# Top 5 posts from r/moviecritic day

## 1. If this film is not 10/10 then, nothing is masterpiece (what's ur 10/10 that fits this phrase?)

**Score:** 597
**Body:** My pick is Barry Lyndon , the world is lucky to have it.

### Top 9 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. Seven Samurai
2. Lawrence of Arabia 
3. 10/10 Western is The Unforgiven.
  - 3:10 to Yuma remake
4. Pride and Prejudice 2005 is very much the same photography.
5. The Princess Bride: perfect casting, exceptional adaptation of a book, dialogue that’s sparkling, and it’s endlessly re-watchable. It’s got everything —Fencing, fighting, torture, revenge, giants, monsters, chases, escapes, true love, and miracles!
6. The Lord of the Rings trilogy. They filmed all three back to back (something that would never happen today). They used miniatures and supplemented with CGI, created sets/costumes that felt “lived in,” composed music that appropriately reflected the scale and scope of middle earth—all of it done so well. It truly feels like a once in a lifetime time cinematic event, especially if you were around when they came out. 
  - Truly lightning in a bottle with this one. 

Enough budget to do it right. Enough talent with costumes, sets, make-up, and effects -- practical and digital -- to make it feel real. Enough dedication from the actors. Enough vision from the director. A score that is epic and memorable. And it somehow managed to dodge outside interference enough that the whole thing was essentially completed before it could be overmanaged.

You can criticize the fact that it does tend toward glorifying the fights more than the books do. which is against theme. But I think that's unavoidable, though it's still valid to comment on. And, you might have wished to see certain scenes changed or characters presented differently, though I think that's the nature of adaptation and I don't think you could reasonably do a more complete version as a set of films.

But it's very difficult to genuinely find fault in the work, rather than to simply disagree with the choices that were made.

# Top 5 posts from r/TrueFilm day

## 1. An under-appreciated aspect of film narrative - before 1960's Psycho, people would just walked into movies at any time, because they would repeat

**Score:** 197
**Body:** One of the most cherished aspects, and somewhat of a mystery of why films of classic Hollywood are so structurally sound in terms of scene writing, blocking and photography, which was lost in later eras, may have at least partially have been explained by how people actually watched films. You didn't necessarily watch films from the beginning. Many would just walk into a film and sit through until they get to the walk-in part again, or sit through it 1.5 times, etc. I'm not sure just how prevalent this was, there's a lot of anecdotal report supporting it, and there is the story that Hitchcock changed it all when [he made an agreement with theater owners to restrict admission](https://www.reddit.com/r/UtterlyInteresting/comments/1oihfii/before_psycho_movie_theaters_didnt_have_fixed/) for Psycho, due to its unique construction. But, if indeed this walk-in habit wasn't rare it probably meant that individual scenes in classic films had to be self-contained narratively. They had to make sense and have a satisfaction that didn't necessarily require knowing the whole story (though that would certainly help). They had to be enjoyable, and readable in their own right. For me, watching films of the 1940s-1950s feel exactly this way. Every scene is tight, has its own internal logic, and I'm always aware of just what is going on in a local way, what kind of person is arguing with what kind of person, the various apparent motivations, and usually the photography itself has its own relish and enjoyment. (The Netflixification of film, which has been apparently been designed around people watching streaming films on open tabs, and with other things going on, solves this problem by having the plot restated over and over again in dialogue, it is said. A very different kind of structural thing, which actually adds to the overall dissatisfaction of straight through film watching.)

This walk-in habit also makes interesting appeals to the idea of watching films like how directors intended them, at least in the Classic Hollywood age, as they must have had start to finish ambitions for film watchers, but they also must have envisioned that people could/would enter a film 25 minutes in, and even might sit through it a 2nd time.

As film start times became more rigid - by now I hate missing even the first seconds of a film even - films themselves must have changed.

\*interestingly enough, when multiplexes came around, kids (and others) started sneaking into second films after they had started, reliving some of that older school film going experience.

Edit in: Taratino captures some of this in his Once Upon A Time In Hollywood, where Sharon Tate notices that the movie she is in is playing across the street. She doesn't care at all what time the film started, she just wants to get in free (ie, be recognized/acknowledged) and watch it. She goes in and just enjoys herself like crazy, like a typical movie goer.

### Top 8 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. The same thing is true for television. Before streaming, you’d rarely start watching a show from the first episode. A scene would caught your eye, and you’d watch whatever part of whatever episode was airing. Part of the fun was trying to figure out what was going on.
  - I remember when Arrested Development was winning Emmys for Season 1, my family decided to give AD a go. The utter confusion of watching "On the Next Arrested Development" and then never seeing those scenes; we always thought we were missing episodes.
2. I started to going to the cinema in the 60s ace yes, it was a looser arrangement. I would often get to a movie halfway through then stay in my seat to watch the next screening so that I could see the first half. I also sneaked between screens in multiplexes. I can remember seeing films on TV (in those days you had to wait 5 years for aTV screening) and realising that I had no recollection of the first minutes but I still considered the film to have been watched. 

Surrealist artists in the 1920s made a whole process out of going to see films after they had started and leaving before the end and going to another one. Therefore any idea of a continuous narrative was destroyed and you were left with random images.
  - >Surrealist artists in the 1920s made a whole process out of going to see films after they had started and leaving before the end and going to another one. Therefore any idea of a continuous narrative was destroyed and you were left with random images.

Wow. That is super interesting. Also because in the 1920s films seemed very episodic in their nature (by my viewing at least), and even less narratively driven than by the time the 1940s came along. Silent film scenes almost felt like small film shorts in their own right. 
3. Hitchcock literally changed the way people thought about going to the movies. People would just go whenever and then stay for the next showing. The first movie I remember seeing was Pinocchio. It was a rerelease. My dad, who was born in 1930, took me to see it. When we got there, they were inside the whale. I didn’t know what was going on. We watched until the end and then waited for it to start again. We watched until we got to the part where they were back inside the whale at which point my dad said “ok, let’s go.”
4. Thank you for bringing up this interesting topic. I teach the history of media, and I am actually going to assign this thread in a future class because there is some great discussion going on.

There are some excellent books, if anybody is interested in the history of the classic Hollywood production system, I have some suggestions below.

One note I would like to make, and this is based partly on memory and partly on scholarship that people have done, is that the moviegoing experience today seems pretty directive. That is, people will say, "I am going to go to the theater to watch BACKROOMS that starts at 6:45pm."

Whereas in the 1940s, absolutely, people might go to watch a particular movie, or they might go to watch a particular star, as in, "There is a new Hedy Lamarr or Humphrey Bogart movie out. Let's go see it." But they also simply "went to the movies." They literally just walked over, drove over, or took a bus to a movie theater, paid admission, and sat down.

If the time they could get there was 5:30, then they saw what was playing at 5:30. If they got there at 6:30 or 7:30 or 8:30, then they just saw whatever was on the screen. They might very well walk in during the middle of a movie, which was okay. They would catch the rest of the movie the next time it came around during their set-aside block of time--maybe next Saturday night. In other words, they were not necessarily arriving at a certain point for the movie. They also had to leave and might well walk out before the ending, again, intending to catch up next time.

So you were not buying admission to a movie as much as admission to a (place) theater and its program. There was some influence here from the older days of vaudeville, where there would be a continuous show of many acts and people would walk in and walk out, as opposed to the "legitimate" theater, where there would be a play and you would go to see the play from the beginning to the end.

I find it interesting, when talking to students, that this is a little bit like watching streaming today, where people might pick something up partway through and use a second screen to find out where they are in the plot. But I do feel that we are still in an era where most people would not want to miss the beginning of a movie and are choosing to watch something from beginning to end.

Although there could be a fascinating discussion about the rise of DNF (completely not finishing) and how common DNF was in 1940 versus today.

I have to think the personality matters as well as culture because I've never been one who is able to stand missing the beginning of a movie.

Bordwell, David, Janet Staiger, and Kristin Thompson. THE CLASSICAL HOLLYWOOD CINEMA: FILM STYLE AND MODE OF PRODUCTION TO 1960. New York: Columbia University Press, 1985.

Gomery, Douglas. THE HOLLYWOOD STUDIO SYSTEM: A HISTORY. New ed. London: British Film Institute, 2005.

Schatz, Thomas. THE GENIUS OF THE SYSTEM: HOLLYWOOD FILMMAKING IN THE STUDIO ERA. New York: Pantheon Books, 1988.
5. I was watching O Brother Where Art Thou the other day and there's a scene where two characters are shown in the cinema, and other characters are shown joining them (in a group) when the movie is already running. I was first like 'wtf why would they bring a whole group into the movie late?' 

The film was set in 1937 so maybe this is part of it.
6. It's not completely true. I checked pre-1960 movie ads in newspapers a few years ago and lots of cinemas did indeed have a certain film on a loop all day where you could seemingly walk in anytime. 

But other cinemas advertised films at certain times: "Film A at 5:00pm, then Film B at 7:30pm", or just one showing: "The Maltese Falcon at 8:00pm" where it would make no sense to walk in after it started because the film wasn't shown again that day. Just like going to see a play.

Maybe Psycho was a causative factor in the former practice dying out generally, while the latter practice expanded and took over.
  - The truth is in between. Theater owners and film makers had been trying to get people to watch movies from the start for ages. The hard part was getting people to do it. I'm sure there were plenty of serious film watchers who always did and they either looked up times or asked the theater. But plenty of people didn't, so it was hard to change the business model. Even with Psycho, it wasn't an overnight shift. There were still plenty of theaters operating on the old model. It took multiplexes to really kill the old habits and even then people occasionally screen hopped. 
7. I didn't know that this was a thing! Very interesting to think about how a simple change like that would change the art form as a whole. I guess the whole concept of a twist or spoiler really hinges on watching linearly. 

## 2. Which movies have an alternative cut, like a Directors Cut, that makes the movie better than the original?

**Score:** 47
**Body:** # I'm not very familiar with different kind of cuts and I don't know whether there's really that many movies that has a Directors Cut or anything similar, but I do remember having seen some discussion about it like 10 years ago, so I just came to think about if there are some movies that actually get better with a particular kind of cut. And are all Extended Editions actually worth the time?

### Top 6 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. Kingdom of Heaven. Generally they're only when the director made too long of a movie for what was contracted, they have to shave it down for time, and in doing so they ruin it. 

Most director's cuts or extended editions are, for me, worse. There's a reason so much is cut out of a movie in the editing phase. It's to make the film tight and efficient, and sometimes clearer. I absolutely hate Apoc. Now Redux for this reason. But it's a good teaching tool, to see "oh yeah, I get why this scene was cut: it's bad." If you have a disc with deleted scenes, watch them, and usually you can see why they were cut.
  - I feel like the newer Final Cut version is a good middle ground between the theatrical and Redux cut of Apocalypse Now. I still think I’d prefer to watch the theatrical though since it’s the shortest version. 
  - Kingdom of Heaven is possibly the greatest example of this.  The extended edition is incredible.
2. The new director’s edition of Star Trek The Motion Picture is vastly superior to the theatrical version. The theatrical version was rushed out to meet a release date and the film never properly finished post production. The Director’s edition  really fine tunes the film.
3. Dark City's theatrical cut had a monologue added at the beginning that gives away a lot of the plot because New Line didn't think audiences would understand it. The director's cut removes it, which a lot of people see as an improvement. (I can't judge it myself because I've only seen the director's cut.)
4. Blade Runner and Kingdom of Heaven are the textbook examples of mid movies becoming masterpieces with director’s cut.

The Lord Of The Rings extended editions for the most part it is agreed it makes for better movies, but it is also agreed there are a handful of poor scenes we could do without or edited with more awareness.

Those are the ones I can think of. 
  - The theatrical version of all 3 LotR movies are the real masterpieces. The extended editions are best if you already love the movies and want more time in the world and with its characters at the cost of pacing.
    - Yeah, I watched the extended versions first because the consensus was that they're better, but I didn't get the hype. Later I watched the theatrical cuts and understood why they're considered such masterpieces.

I do think Saruman's arc conclusion should have stayed in the theatrical versions instead of being cut and have that plotline abandoned 
    - I personally for the most part always enjoyed the slower pacing way more as it matches the cozy feeling of reading the books, but you're right, book readers are biased, and for the most part the pacing is better in theatrical release
5. I liked Midsommar’s directors cut, which was pretty minimal in terms of added content, but added a few scenes which I felt really fleshed out the dynamics between the protagonist and her boyfriend.

## 3. Why do some movies just disappear?

**Score:** 44
**Body:** I’m a big fan of French-Algerian director Tony Gatlif. His movies usually screen at the European festivals and then disappear, and I don’t understand why.

Here’s a list of prices he’s won:

Cannes Film Festival (2004): Best Director for Exils.  
Cannes Film Festival (1993): Un Certain Regard Award for Latcho Drom.  
Locarno Film Festival (1997): Silver Leopard and Prize of the Ecumenical Jury for Gadjo Dilo (The Crazy Stranger).  
César Awards: Best Original Music for Gadjo Dilo (1997).  
CineFest Miskolc International Film Festival (2021): Lifetime Achievement Award.

I remember renting his movies Gadjo Dilo and Latcho Drom back in the video store days, and I’ve found most, but not all, of his other movies online in less than stellar quality—often without subtitles—on sites I maybe wouldn’t recommend using. They don’t stream anywhere, at least not in my area (Sweden, plus international services). The physical releases consist of out-of-stock DVDs.

Is it just the fact that he’s not that popular? Are the movies stuck in some kind of copyright hell? What do you think? I can't find any information online. He's even still active; it's not like he made a couple of movies a hundred years ago and disappeared.

I guess I’m just bitter that some of my favorite movies ever aren’t available in good quality anywhere.

Simply speaking, it is either not lucrative enough to make DVD copies of them, or there’s not interest for a streaming platform. That’s usually what happens to a lot of non-Hollywood films, most films are probably not commercially-viable enough to get big distribution.

Its a matter of distribution, a lot of films just dont get distribution. Having said this, often if you manage to contact the production company or the director they can be kind enough to send you a link where you can watch their film!

## 4. Films that have really distinct editing styles?

**Score:** 36
**Body:** I was just rewatching The Big Short last night and found the editing style to be much more intentional and effective than it was in McKay’s later works, where he continued to use techniques like the hold-frames or inserting other still images, but it didn’t feel nearly effective in Vice/Dont Look Up in my opinion.

I was also listening to the soundtrack for the movie Jackie, which I was pleasantly surprised to see was done by Mica Levi, who did my favorite film score of all time, Under the Skin. I haven’t seen Jackie in quite a long time, but I do remember it having a very effective, intentionally disorienting editing style. My best way of describing it is it feels like the movie itself is in shock.

Just looking for other films which really use deliberate editing choices as a storytelling tool.

### Top 9 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. I'd like to wager the Ocean's Trilogy (Especially Ocean's Eleven), which really captures the 'coolness' of the entire crew through its clever blocking and editing work, especially the transitions. Might not be as obvious as some of your examples, but I really think the editing adds a lot to the suaveness of the film.

In a similar vein, Lock Stock and Two Smoking Barrels and Snatch are also really interesting in terms of the way they blend voiceover, freeze frames and different storylines. Guy Ritchie really peaked with those films, has gotten nowhere near those heights since. 
2. Run Lola Run. It uses split screen, going over the same scene later from a different point of view, unusual camera angles, slo-mo, even cartoons to illustrate the action and emotional experience of the characters. And it's also one of those movie stories that takes place over a single 24 hour period.
3. All That Jazz is one of the best edited movies I've ever seen. Whiplash is also terrifically done. It's an anime and it may be more the pacing than editing, but Perfect Blue is incredibly well done and disorienting.
4. The Limey (1999): Editing basically transforms the film from a by-the-numbers revenge thriller (*Death Wish* in LA) to a haunting reflection on loss and redemption, also by incorporating clips from an earlier Terence Stamp film.

Don't Look Now (1973): Uses fragmented editing in both supernatural and apparently mundane scenes, conveying both the distorted worldview that comes with grief and the terrifying encounter with the unknown.

  - I’ve seen Scott Pilgrim probably close to twenty times lol. I was absolutely obsessed with it in middle school and showed it to damn near anyone who would sit through it.
6. Uncut Gems (2019), which ironically enough is intensely, intensely cut. It really serves to forward the general (seeming) premise of the natural world or beauty being cut like a gem to show glittering facets, and the brutal source of the mining of gems that fuels capitalism. The cuts ARE like gem-cuts.
7. I don't know if this answers you're question exactly, but Psycho has a very intentional and clever editing. There's not really any gore but it still stays horrifying and shocking thanks to the way Hitchcock edited. 
8. Gotta watch F For Fake, arguably Orson Welles’ masterpiece, and possibly the most uniquely edited film I’ve ever seen. It’s a blend of documentary, essay and narrative, and Welles frequently cuts back to himself in the editing bay to rewind, pause and re-interrogate the footage we’ve just seen.

It’s so brilliant that it feels almost effortless, but is an incredible show of mastery of the form, and an understanding of how editing can shape the rhythm, meaning and interpretation of what we’re seeing.
